ideas.title: Blow your own bubble in Jump in
ideas.critique: The film of a glob swelling and darkening is what the last post already showed, so the step that counts is the player's breath and the clock. A GPU solver fast enough to play, with a real pop when a wall gets thin, is new to the game. If the film is only the gather sagging again, it reads as a repeat.

ideas.title: Prince Rupert's drops
ideas.nearest: Chipping a stone to change its note
ideas.critique: Quench stress deciding how a thing shatters is new physics, and a slow-motion traced burst into glittering glass is very clippable. The risk is that the fragmentation turns into a scripted particle puff instead of a crack running through a solved stress field. Once the magic is known, play is drip, snip, burst, and there is little to vary.

ideas.title: A window from your broken glass
ideas.critique: Coloured light crawling across the floor through the day shows off the path tracer well. But the 2D shard puzzle is a placement minigame with no physics, and it depends on enough real failed pieces existing first. Underneath, it is a new prop in the cottage, watched slowly.

ideas.title: One stone in the surf
ideas.critique: Shallow water with sediment transport sorting three coloured sands is a simulation the island has never had, and striped sand building up behind a stone is a sight worth showing. It is honest that it is a test. It belongs to a different big goal, though, and setting one stone is a toy you watch, not yet a game.

ideas.title: A stick that bends and snaps
ideas.nearest: Chipping a stone to change its note
ideas.critique: A rod that breaks where it bends most, with stiffness that depends on moisture, is a real material and a base for later building. Its weakness is Lumi's beak: if the levering and the knee bend look like a puppet pushing a rod, the strong physics gets lost. A stick snapping is also a familiar sight in games.

ideas.title: Throw a pot on the kick wheel
ideas.critique: It sits right at the core of the big goal, and the player's own profile with glaze pooling in their own cuts is a payoff they get to keep. But the glaze flow and the jar have already been shown, so the film's ending is predictable. Only the hand-driven wheel is new.

ideas.title: Drink from what you made
ideas.critique: Water spilling over a crooked cup's real low rim onto a friend is a lovely test of a shape, and it ties the friends to the made thing. Running FLIP inside a small vessel at playable cost is unproven, and the creatures drinking will probably be scripted. It also needs vessels the player made before it means anything.

ideas.title: Lumi falls for real
ideas.critique: Ragdoll falls with a blend back to getting up are a standard game technique, so it will look expected to anyone who has played games. Getting the blend right without pops is hard and has real value for animation. Its link to holding things in the big goal is thin.

ideas.title: A fold that stays
ideas.critique: Plastic hinges that keep a crease are exactly the 'fold that creases paper for good' in the big goal, and a sheet springing half back is honest physics. Much of the step is profiling, which is invisible. A folded paper boat as the film is the predictable picture.

ideas.title: Lightning glass on the beach
ideas.critique: Laplacian growth carving a branching glass root is a genuinely strange, real thing, and each bolt makes its own shape. But the player does nothing except dig it up and hang it on a wall, and it rests on a storm event, so it is mostly something to look at. Here the island made the glass, not the player's hands.
